title: Where the prior comes from: pre-test probability in your own clinic

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The prior probability of a condition for a patient, also called the pre-test probability, is the probability that a person like this patient, in this setting, has the condition before the test result is known.

You estimate it as a proportion, in the sense of Book 0, A5. Divide the number of people who had the condition by the number examined, in a stated group over a stated period. Four things fix which proportion is the right one.

  1. The condition must be defined exactly as it was in the study that measured the sensitivity and specificity: the same reference test and the same cut-off.
  2. The denominator must be the people to whom the test will be applied.
  3. The people must be like this patient in what changes the prevalence: age, sex, setting, and why they came.
  4. The count must come from a stated period, with every person tested by the reference test, not only those who were suspected.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Bayes’ theorem needs a starting chance. That chance is how common the condition is among people like your patient, where you see them.

Nobody hands you that number. You count it. Take the people your clinic would test. Count how many turned out to have the condition. Divide by how many there were.

A national figure, a figure from a study and a figure from your own register are three different groups. Use the group your patient belongs to.

blocks.alt: A rising curve through five points: PPV 8.73 per cent at a prior of 5, 16.89 at 10.06, 25.00 at 15.5, 31.24 at 20 and 43.78 at 30. A dashed line at 17.0 marks the paper's printed PPV.
blocks.caption: The positive predictive value of an Indian Diabetes Risk Score of 60 or more, at five priors, with sensitivity 72.5 per cent and specificity 60.1 per cent held fixed. At the prior worked out from the paper’s counts, about 10.06 per cent, it is 16.89, close to the printed 17.0. The overall prevalence of 15.5 per cent, which includes people already known to have diabetes, would give 25.00.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a printed predictive value and try to rebuild it. Open “A simplified Indian Diabetes Risk Score for screening for undiagnosed diabetic subjects” by Mohan and colleagues (2005), at https://repository.ias.ac.in/80170/. The Indian Diabetes Risk Score (IDRS) adds points for age, waist, physical activity and family history. Search for “optimum sensitivity”.

An IDRS value ≥ 60 had the optimum sensitivity (72.5%) and specificity (60.1%) for determining diabetes. The positive predictive value was 17.0%

The sign ≥ is read “greater than or equal to”. So a score of 60 or more has sensitivity 72.5 per cent and specificity 60.1 per cent, and a PPV of 17.0 per cent. Here PPV is the positive predictive value of Book 0, D3: the share of positive results that are right. A PPV belongs to a prior. Which prior gives 17.0?

The first number you meet is in the Results. Search for “overall prevalence”.

Overall, 365 of the 2350 study subjects had diabetes (overall prevalence: 15.5%

Try 15.5 per cent as the prior, in the PPV formula of section 5. The false-positive rate is 1 minus the specificity.

1 minus 0.601 = 0.399
1 minus 0.155 = 0.845
0.725 times 0.155 = 0.112375
0.399 times 0.845 = 0.337155
0.112375 plus 0.337155 = 0.44953
0.112375 divided by 0.44953 = 0.24998…

About 25.0 per cent. The paper says 17.0. Something about the prior is wrong.

Read on one sentence.

For developing the diabetes risk score, 143 subjects with known diabetes in Phase 3 were excluded.

The 365 includes people who already knew they had diabetes. Nobody screens them, and the score was never applied to them. Take them out of both the top and the bottom.

365 minus 143 = 222
2350 minus 143 = 2207
222 divided by 2207 = 0.10058…

About 10.06 per cent. The legend of the paper’s Fig. 1 gives the same number analysed, n = 2,207. Now the formula again.

1 minus 0.1006 = 0.8994
0.725 times 0.1006 = 0.072935
0.399 times 0.8994 = 0.3588606
0.072935 plus 0.3588606 = 0.4317956
0.072935 divided by 0.4317956 = 0.16891…

About 16.9 per cent. The printed sensitivity and specificity are rounded, so 16.9 against 17.0 is as close as they allow. The paper’s own Discussion uses the same prior, from the Chennai Urban Rural Epidemiology Study (CURES), a population survey in Chennai: “the prevalence of undiagnosed diabetes … observed in CURES i.e. 10.1%”.

So the 17.0 per cent is the PPV among people in Chennai not yet known to have diabetes. It is tied to a prior of about 10 per cent. The 15.5 per cent was a real prevalence too. It was the prevalence of the wrong group.

The table puts the same score at five priors. Each row is the PPV formula with 0.725 and 0.399, and the prior in per cent.

prior (%) PPV of IDRS 60 or more (%)
5 8.73
10.06 16.89
15.5 25.00
20 31.24
30 43.78

The score’s sensitivity and specificity do not change down the table. The PPV changes more than fivefold.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The formula reproduces 17.0 only on the assumption that the sensitivity and specificity hold at every prior. They were measured on one Chennai sample, CURES Phase 3, at one time. In a clinic where the people tested differ in how the score behaves, the table is a guide, not a measurement.

The 10.06 per cent is worked out from the paper’s counts. The paper never prints it as the prior of its PPV; the match with 17.0 is what shows it was.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now the arm tape of Book 0, D3, and three places you might take its prior from. In Kiran and colleagues’ study the tape’s cut-off for men was 31.3 cm, with sensitivity 86 per cent and specificity 74 per cent. Those figures fit the 42 men with a body-mass index from 25 to 29.9, as Book 0 found. So the condition the tape was tested against is “in the 25 to 29.9 band”.

First, the study’s own men. 42 of 131 were in the band, about 32 per cent, and Book 0’s rebuilt table gave a PPV of about 61 per cent. That prior describes medical students in one Mangaluru college. Your clinic is not that college.

Second, the national survey. The India fact sheet of the sixth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-6, 2023-24) gives 27.3 per cent of men aged 15 to 49 as having overweight or obesity (a body-mass index of 25 or more). Put it in the formula and you get a number.

1 minus 0.273 = 0.727
0.86 times 0.273 = 0.23478
0.26 times 0.727 = 0.18902
0.23478 plus 0.18902 = 0.4238
0.23478 divided by 0.4238 = 0.55398…

About 55 per cent. Before you use it, run the four checks of the definition. The survey counts a body-mass index of 25 or more. The tape’s figures fit the 25 to 29.9 band only. So the first check fails: the prior and the test are about different conditions. The survey’s men are all of India’s men aged 15 to 49, so the third check fails too for most clinics. The 55 per cent is arithmetic on a prior that answers a different question.

Third, your own register. Suppose, as a made-up example, that your urban health centre measured every man aged 18 to 29 who came to its outpatient clinic from April to September. The register shows 480 men, all weighed and measured, and 96 of them in the 25 to 29.9 band.

96 divided by 480 = 0.2

The prior is 0.2, one in five. That is the stated group of Book 0, so its PPV is already known: about 45 per cent.

0.86 times 0.2 = 0.172
0.26 times 0.8 = 0.208
0.172 plus 0.208 = 0.38
0.172 divided by 0.38 = 0.45263…

Three sources gave about 61, 55 and 45 per cent for the same tape. Only the last answers the question a man at your clinic asks. It has the right condition, the right people and a stated period, and every man in it was measured.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The register is made up, and so is its count of 96 of 480. A real register gives the right prior only if everyone in it was measured. A register that records body-mass index only for men who looked heavy has counted the suspected, and its prevalence is too high.

Every PPV here also assumes the tape’s sensitivity and specificity carry from the Mangaluru students to your clinic. That is the subject of the next illustration.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
The prior is not the only estimate in the formula. The tape’s sensitivity of 86 per cent is 36 of the 42 men in the band, from Book 0’s rebuilt table. Its specificity of 74 per cent is 66 of the 89 men outside it. Each is a count from one small sample, so each would have come out a little differently in another sample of students.

How much does one man matter? Suppose the tape had caught 35 of the 42, or 37. Keep the specificity at 66 of 89, and your clinic’s prior at 0.2.

35 divided by 42 = 0.8333…
37 divided by 42 = 0.88095…
66 divided by 89 = 0.74157…
1 minus 0.7416 = 0.2584
0.8333 times 0.2 = 0.16666
0.2584 times 0.8 = 0.20672
0.16666 plus 0.20672 = 0.37338
0.16666 divided by 0.37338 = 0.44635…
0.8810 times 0.2 = 0.1762
0.1762 plus 0.20672 = 0.38292
0.1762 divided by 0.38292 = 0.46015…

One man either way moves the PPV from about 44.6 to about 46.0 per cent. Let one man move in the specificity too, 65 or 67 of 89, and the nine combinations run from about 43.6 to about 47.1 per cent. Another sample of the same size could easily differ by more than one man.

So write the PPV as “about 45 per cent”, not “45.26 per cent”. The digits after the point are arithmetic, not knowledge. How wide the honest range is comes from the sampling distribution of the sensitivity and specificity, how they would vary from one sample of the same size to the next, which the next book of this subject teaches.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
Moving one man is an illustration of size, not an interval. It does not say how far another sample would actually land; that needs the sampling distribution, taught in the next book of this subject.

The 36 and 66 are Book 0’s rebuilt counts, not counts the paper prints. And a sample of medical students is not your clinic, which no count from it can repair.

points.html: “Use the national prevalence as the prior for my patient” is the error.

Before you put any prevalence into Bayes’ theorem, run four checks aloud. Same condition and cut-off as the test’s study? Denominator only the people you would test? People like your patient? A stated period, with everyone tested? If one fails, say so beside the answer.
Count your own prior from your register: the number with the condition, the number examined, and the months covered.
A prevalence that includes people already known to have the condition is the wrong prior for a screening test.
A register that records the condition only for people who were suspected gives a prior that is too high. Then every PPV you work from it is too high too.
The PPV you work out carries the error of three estimates: the prior, the sensitivity and the specificity.
When a paper prints a PPV, find the prior it belongs to before you quote it.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “The test’s PPV is 17 per cent, so 17 per cent of my positives will have diabetes.” The 17.0 per cent belongs to the prior it was worked out at, about 10 per cent in the IDRS paper. At a prior of 5 per cent the same score gives about 8.7 per cent; at 20 per cent, about 31 per cent. Find your own prior, then work out your own PPV.

blocks.label: Reporting it
blocks.html: Pre-test probability: (the count) of (the number examined) (the people, defined as the test’s study defined them), examined at (the clinic) from (month) to (month), had (the condition), or (the per cent) per cent. With the sensitivity and specificity reported by (the study), a positive result raises this to about (the per cent) per cent. Both figures are estimates; treat them as approximate.

blocks.prompt: From memory: what is the prior probability for a patient, how do you estimate it, and what four checks must the number pass before you put it into Bayes’ theorem?
blocks.answer:
The prior is the probability that a person like this patient, in this setting, has the condition before the test result is known.

Estimate it as a proportion: the number who had the condition, divided by the number examined, in a stated group over a stated period.

The four checks:

  1. The condition is defined as in the test’s study, with the same reference test and cut-off.
  2. The denominator holds only people the test would be applied to. People already known to have the condition are left out.
  3. The people are like your patient in age, sex, setting and why they came.
  4. The count covers a stated period, and everyone in it was examined, not only the suspected.

blocks.prompt:
You are preparing the Bayes handout for one test used in your own clinic. Plan how you will get its prior.

Write down six things.

  1. The condition, defined as the test’s study defined it.
  2. The register you will use.
  3. Who goes in the denominator, and who you will leave out.
  4. The period.
  5. How you will check that everyone in the denominator was examined.
  6. The one sentence the handout will print about where the prior came from.
blocks.answer:
A good plan names each item concretely.

The condition matches the study. For IDRS it is diabetes newly found by a 2-hour plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or more, the World Health Organization criterion Mohan and colleagues used in 2005. It is not “diabetes” from any record.

The register is one in which the reference test was done. For IDRS that is a screening register with a glucose result against every name. A clinic list of people already on treatment is not enough.

The denominator is the people the test would be used on. For IDRS, adults not already known to have diabetes. Leave out known cases, and say how many you left out.

The period is stated, such as April to September, and long enough to hold more than a handful of cases. With five cases, one more or less moves the prior by a fifth.

The check: count how many in the denominator have a result for the reference test. If some do not, the prior is uncertain, and in which direction depends on who was skipped. Say so.

The sentence, for example: “Pre-test probability: 27 of 260 adults not known to have diabetes, screened with a glucose test at this centre from April to September, had diabetes (about 10 per cent).” The counts in that sentence are made up; yours come from your register.

blocks.prompt:
Three numbers are offered as “the prevalence of overweight in young men” for the arm-tape handout. NFHS-6 gives 27.3 per cent. Kiran and colleagues’ men give 32 per cent. A made-up clinic register gives 20 per cent, 96 of 480 men.

For each, say what kind of number it is, a survey estimate of a national parameter or a proportion in one sample, and which group it describes. Then say which one belongs in the handout, and why.
blocks.answer:
The NFHS-6 figure, 27.3 per cent, is a survey estimate of a parameter. The parameter is the share of all men aged 15 to 49 in India with a body-mass index of 25 or more, in 2023 to 2024. It describes India’s men, not your clinic’s. Its condition, 25 or more, is not the tape’s condition, the 25 to 29.9 band.

Kiran and colleagues’ 32 per cent is a proportion in one sample: 42 of 131 male medical students in one college, in the 25 to 29.9 band. It estimates the prevalence among students like them, and the sample was not drawn at random from any wider group.

The register’s 20 per cent is a proportion among the men measured at your clinic in one period. It estimates the prevalence among men who come to your clinic.

The register figure belongs in the handout. It has the right condition, the right people and a stated period, provided every man in it was measured. The other two are true of their own groups.

blocks.prompt:
A register lists 600 people examined in a year, and 45 of them had the condition.

Work out the prevalence as a proportion and as a per cent.
blocks.answer:
45 divided by 600 = 0.075
0.075 times 100 = 7.5

The prevalence is 0.075, or 7.5 per cent.

blocks.prompt:
A test has sensitivity 0.8 and specificity 0.9.

Work out its PPV at a prior of 0.05 and at a prior of 0.2.
blocks.answer:
The false-positive rate is 1 minus 0.9, which is 0.1.

At 0.05:

0.8 times 0.05 = 0.04
0.1 times 0.95 = 0.095
0.04 plus 0.095 = 0.135
0.04 divided by 0.135 = 0.2962…

At 0.2:

0.8 times 0.2 = 0.16
0.1 times 0.8 = 0.08
0.16 plus 0.08 = 0.24
0.16 divided by 0.24 = 0.6666…

About 0.30 at a prior of 0.05, and about 0.67 at 0.2. The test did not change.

blocks.prompt:
A test has sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.8. A paper reports its PPV as 0.5.

Work out the prior the paper’s PPV belongs to.
blocks.answer:
Use the odds form of section 8. The positive likelihood ratio (LR+) is the sensitivity divided by 1 minus the specificity.

1 minus 0.8 = 0.2
0.9 divided by 0.2 = 4.5

A PPV of 0.5 is posterior odds of 0.5 divided by 0.5, which is 1. Prior odds times 4.5 gives 1, so the prior odds are 1 divided by 4.5.

1 divided by 4.5 = 0.2222…
0.2222 divided by 1.2222 = 0.1818…

The prior is about 0.18. Check it.

0.9 times 0.1818 = 0.16362
0.2 times 0.8182 = 0.16364
0.16362 divided by 0.32726 = 0.49997…

About 0.5, as reported.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up register from a primary health centre covers April to June. It lists 300 adults screened with a glucose test. Of these, 40 already knew they had diabetes, and 27 others were newly found to have it.

You want the prior for the Indian Diabetes Risk Score in this centre. Work it out as a per cent, and say who is in the denominator.
blocks.answer:
The score is used to find undiagnosed diabetes, so leave out the 40 who already knew.

300 minus 40 = 260
27 divided by 260 = 0.10384…

The prior is about 10.4 per cent: 27 of the 260 adults screened from April to June who did not already know they had diabetes.

The tempting answer is 67 of 300, about 22.3 per cent. That counts people the score would never be used on.

blocks.prompt:
The Indian Diabetes Risk Score at 60 or more has sensitivity 72.5 per cent and specificity 60.1 per cent (Mohan and colleagues, 2005). In a rural camp your prior for undiagnosed diabetes is 5 per cent.

Work out the PPV of a score of 60 or more in the camp, as a per cent.
blocks.answer:
1 minus 0.601 = 0.399
1 minus 0.05 = 0.95
0.725 times 0.05 = 0.03625
0.399 times 0.95 = 0.37905
0.03625 plus 0.37905 = 0.4153
0.03625 divided by 0.4153 = 0.08728…

About 8.7 per cent. Fewer than one in eleven people with a score of 60 or more in this camp will have undiagnosed diabetes, against 17.0 per cent in the paper’s Chennai sample.

blocks.prompt:
In Book 0’s rebuilt table, Kiran and colleagues’ arm tape caught 36 of 42 men in the 25 to 29.9 band and cleared 66 of 89 men outside it. Your clinic’s prior is 0.2.

Keep the sensitivity at 36 of 42. Work out the PPV with the specificity at 65 of 89 and at 67 of 89. Then say how many digits of the PPV you would print.
blocks.answer:
36 divided by 42 = 0.8571…
0.8571 times 0.2 = 0.17142
65 divided by 89 = 0.7303…
1 minus 0.7303 = 0.2697
0.2697 times 0.8 = 0.21576
0.17142 plus 0.21576 = 0.38718
0.17142 divided by 0.38718 = 0.44274…
67 divided by 89 = 0.7528…
1 minus 0.7528 = 0.2472
0.2472 times 0.8 = 0.19776
0.17142 plus 0.19776 = 0.36918
0.17142 divided by 0.36918 = 0.46432…

About 44.3 per cent and 46.4 per cent. One man either way in the specificity moves the PPV by about one percentage point each way. Print “about 45 per cent”. A second decimal would claim a precision a sample of 89 men cannot give.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer from a draft handout. Find the step that broke.

IDRS 60 or more: sensitivity 0.725, specificity 0.601
prior: diabetes in CURES Phase 3, 365 of 2350 = 0.155
0.725 times 0.155 = 0.112375
0.399 times 0.845 = 0.337155
PPV = 0.112375 divided by 0.449530 = 0.25
so a quarter of people with a score of 60 or more have undiagnosed diabetes
blocks.answer:
The second line broke. The 365 includes 143 people who already knew they had diabetes. The score is never applied to them, so they belong in neither the top nor the bottom.

365 minus 143 = 222
2350 minus 143 = 2207
222 divided by 2207 = 0.1006…
0.725 times 0.1006 = 0.072935
0.399 times 0.8994 = 0.3588606
0.072935 divided by 0.4317956 = 0.1689…

About 16.9 per cent, which matches the paper’s printed 17.0 within rounding. The draft’s 25 per cent overstates it by half again.

Why it looks reasonable: 15.5 per cent is printed in the Results as “overall prevalence”, and the arithmetic after it is right. The error is in which group the prior describes.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

arm tape for men, cut-off 31.3 cm: sensitivity 0.86, specificity 0.74
prior: NFHS-6, men aged 15-49 with overweight or obesity, 0.273
0.86 times 0.273 = 0.23478
0.26 times 0.727 = 0.18902
PPV = 0.23478 divided by 0.4238 = 0.55
so more than half the men the tape flags in my clinic have a body-mass index of 25 or more
blocks.answer:
Every line of arithmetic is right. The prior is the step that broke, in two ways.

First, the condition. The tape’s 86 and 74 per cent fit the men in the 25 to 29.9 band, as Book 0 found. NFHS-6’s 27.3 per cent counts everyone at 25 or more. The prior and the test describe different conditions. So the last line’s “25 or more” is not what the formula computed.

Second, the people. 27.3 per cent is all of India’s men aged 15 to 49. Your clinic’s men may be older, more urban, or there for reasons linked to weight. Use your register’s count for men like your patients, in the band, over a stated period.

Why it looks reasonable: NFHS-6 is the most trusted prevalence in India, and it is a real number about the right sex. It is the prevalence of a different group and a different condition.

blocks.prompt:
A camp coordinator writes this in a note to the medical officer.

The IDRS paper gives a positive predictive value of 17 per cent. So in our camp at the diabetes awareness rally, about one in six people with a score of 60 or more will have undiagnosed diabetes.

Suppose, for this problem only, that undiagnosed diabetes among people who come to such a rally is 20 per cent. Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: the PPV at the camp’s own prior, with the paper’s sensitivity and specificity.

1 minus 0.2 = 0.8
0.725 times 0.2 = 0.145
0.399 times 0.8 = 0.3192
0.145 plus 0.3192 = 0.4642
0.145 divided by 0.4642 = 0.31236…

About 31 per cent: nearer one in three than one in six. The note carried the paper’s PPV to a group with twice the paper’s prior.

What it does not establish. The 20 per cent is a supposition; the camp’s real prior has to be counted. The sensitivity and specificity were measured in a Chennai population sample. People who come to an awareness rally may differ, so the score may behave differently in them. And no PPV says which of the people with a high score have diabetes. Each still needs the glucose test.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague says this at a review meeting.

Our handout should use the national figure. NFHS-6 says 30.7 per cent of women have overweight or obesity. That’s the most reliable number we have, so it’s the right prior for every woman we measure with the arm tape.

For women, Kiran and colleagues’ cut-off is 28.5 cm, with sensitivity 88 per cent and specificity 83 per cent. Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what the answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
What to compute: what the handout would print with the colleague’s prior, and what it would print with a different one, to show how much rides on the choice.

1 minus 0.83 = 0.17
1 minus 0.307 = 0.693
0.88 times 0.307 = 0.27016
0.17 times 0.693 = 0.11781
0.27016 plus 0.11781 = 0.38797
0.27016 divided by 0.38797 = 0.69634…
0.88 times 0.1 = 0.088
0.17 times 0.9 = 0.153
0.088 plus 0.153 = 0.241
0.088 divided by 0.241 = 0.36514…

About 70 per cent at a prior of 0.307, and about 37 per cent at 0.1. The choice of prior moves the answer by about 33 percentage points.

What to say back. “Most reliable” is about how well NFHS-6 estimates its own figure: women aged 15 to 49 across India, body-mass index 25 or more. It says nothing about whether that is the prevalence among the women at this clinic. The right prior is counted from the clinic’s own register, for women like the patients, with the condition defined as the test’s study defined it. And the condition differs here too. The 88 and 83 fit the 41 women in the 25 to 29.9 band. NFHS-6 counts everyone at 25 or more.

What this does not establish. The 0.1 is a supposition chosen to show the effect. The tape’s figures come from medical students in one college. And a reliable national number is not a wrong one: it is the right prior for a national question.
